source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Earlier reports that self-critique helps came from using the true answer label to decide when to stop. With the label, accuracy rises. Without it, the same method does not help.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle label: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4 with oracle: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. GSM8K on full test set; CSQA n=200; HotpotQA n=100.
limits: Reasoning tasks with single checkable answers; 2023-era models; a critique prompt, not a trained red team.
agent_relevance: A red-team step that knows the right answer is not a test of red teaming. Only count critique gains measured without a label (G2, G3).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no label, no tool) lowered accuracy on almost every model and task over two rounds.
limits: Prompts follow Kim et al. 2023 / Shinn et al. 2023; HotpotQA sample is only 100 items.
agent_relevance: Forcing the agent to challenge its own answer on a schedule costs accuracy. Challenge only on a signal (G1).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: A weaker open model is hurt more. Different red-team style prompts did not fix this.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0, CSQA 84.0 -> 81.5 -> 83.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5, CSQA 64.0 -> 37.5 -> 36.5. The prompt 'Assume this answer could be either correct or incorrect... report any serious problems' gave 88.0 then 90.0 on GSM8K, no gain.
limits: Only three feedback prompts tested per model.
agent_relevance: Even the exact 'assume it may be wrong' devil's-advocate wording failed. The loss grows as the base model gets weaker.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Why it fails: the model cannot judge its own reasoning, so it flips right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; of the changes, correct-to-incorrect exceeded incorrect-to-correct. On CSQA the model changed answers far more often because wrong options look relevant.
limits: Flip counts read from a bar chart; exact counts not in text.
agent_relevance: Any critic must be paired with a check that locates a real fault (G2); a critic that only voices doubt will mostly create flips.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2023 prompts) was re-run on the whole GSM8K test set. At equal numbers of responses, plain majority vote beat debate.
numbers: Standard prompt 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate (3 agents, 2 rounds) about 83 at 6 to 9 responses.
limits: Table text extracted from a PDF with merged columns; debate values are approximate. Original Du et al. used only 100 items.
agent_relevance: Supports G9: debate is a costly form of sampling. Spend the same tokens on independent samples plus a vote.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmark of debate protocols (Society of Mind, ChatEval, Multi-Persona with a 'devil' agent, Ensemble Refinement) against single-agent baselines on six datasets. Debate did not reliably beat self-consistency or Medprompt, and cost more calls.
numbers: On three medical sets every system but Multi-Persona beat single agent; self-consistency and Medprompt were best. On three non-medical sets single-agent methods beat all systems except Multi-Persona and self-consistency. Multi-Persona (second agent told to disagree) lowered accuracy versus the first agent's answer.
limits: GPT-3.5-class models; default hyperparameters; sensitivity checked with K-fold over datasets.
agent_relevance: The angel-and-devil red-team pair is the weakest debate form at default settings. Forced disagreement can wreck a correct first answer.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: How hard the devil is told to disagree is a large moderator. High agreement helped on knowledge questions; low agreement helped on a counter-intuitive reasoning set.
numbers: On a 376-question USMLE subset, raising prompted agreement intensity gave about +15% for Multi-Persona and +5% for Society of Mind; ChatEval hardly changed. Multi-Persona at 90% agreement became best protocol on full MedQA, beating Medprompt and self-consistency. On CIAR (counter-intuitive) the trend reversed: more disagreement was better.
limits: Tuned per dataset, so the best level is not known in advance.
agent_relevance: Red-team strength should depend on how likely the first answer is wrong. A fixed adversary is wrong for easy items and right for trap items; set it by a signal.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: One agent with a strong prompt (task description, answer description, demonstrations) matches the best multi-agent discussion. Discussion helped only when the prompt had no demonstrations.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5, average over ECQA, GSM8K, FOLIO-wiki. No demo: single 67.41, MAD(3) 63.42, Debate(3) 71.67, Debate(6) 69.38, CMD(6) 70.75. With demo: single 75.63, MAD 70.04, Debate(3) 73.88, Debate(6) 72.26, CMD(6) 74.46.
limits: Small test samples (100 items for some sets); one backbone in the main table.
agent_relevance: Debate gain is a substitute for missing context. If the scaffold already gives worked examples and a clear task, adversarial rounds add little.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk isn't always cheap: failure modes in multi-agent debate
finding: Debate can lower accuracy below majority vote and below the starting answers, and accuracy can fall round by round. Mixing a weak agent with strong agents hurt the strong ones.
numbers: CommonsenseQA, MMLU, GSM8K with GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B in mixed groups; correct-to-incorrect flips exceeded incorrect-to-correct flips, and flip chance rose with the number of peers who disagreed (shown in figures; no exact table in text).
limits: Small open models; effect depends on dataset and mix.
agent_relevance: Social pressure inside the model: agents prefer agreement over challenge. Do not let adversary and answerer talk; feed critic output into code checks.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Assistants cave when challenged, even when right. A challenge-heavy loop can trigger this.
numbers: After 'I don't think that's right. Are you sure?', Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted mistakes on 98% of questions where it had been right (as stated in the paper); accuracy fell by up to 27% on average over six datasets. A user suggesting a wrong answer cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). Five assistants tested.
limits: RLHF-tuned 2023 assistants; newer models may differ.
agent_relevance: A critic's challenge can look to the answerer like a user challenge. Make the answerer revise only against failing output (G2), never against the mere presence of doubt.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with more persuasive LLMs leads to more truthful answers
finding: Structured two-sided debate helps a weak judge when the debaters see a source text the judge cannot. A positive result for adversarial argument.
numbers: Non-expert LLM judges 76% with debate vs 48% naive baseline; human judges 88% vs 60% baseline (QuALITY reading questions). Judge accuracy in static debate 86% to 92% across settings. Interactive protocol rejecting judgments under 75% confidence kept 65% of questions at 94% accuracy.
limits: Needs an information gap: debaters have evidence, judge does not. Same-information debate (Huang, Wynn) does not show the gain.
agent_relevance: Adversarial structure pays when the critic holds evidence the judge lacks, such as code output or retrieved text. Matches G2 and G8.

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red teaming language models with language models
finding: An LM can generate test cases that find failures in another LM. Zero-shot generation finds few; reinforcement learning finds many but narrow ones.
numbers: 0.5M zero-shot test cases drew an offensive reply 3.7% of the time; RL-trained red LM drew offensive replies from the 280B dialogue model over 40% of the time, with lower diversity.
limits: Target was harm, not reasoning errors; judged by a classifier.
agent_relevance: Generated adversarial inputs are useful when a classifier or program judges the result. Diversity must be enforced or the attack set collapses to one trick.

source: Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents (2024)
finding: An agent that asks 'what if this action fails' before acting, and checks after each subtask, scored best among the compared web agents.
numbers: WebArena success after seven episodes: anticipatory reflection 23.5%, LATS 22.7%, Plan+Act 19.8%. Plan revisions fell 45%. First-trial actions 6.39 vs 4.01 for Plan+Act.
limits: Gap to LATS is 0.8 points with no confidence interval; one benchmark; no plain-retry ablation seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Pre-action doubt tied to a concrete next step (what would break this subgoal) is cheap and may help. It differs from scheduled global doubt, and the margin is small.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Conversational agents as catalysts for critical thinking
finding: Human groups with an LLM devil's advocate reported better process and outcome satisfaction, but psychological safety did not change significantly.
numbers: 48 participants, 12 groups of 4 (one senior, one junior). Process satisfaction 5.10 to 5.55 (p<0.01); outcome satisfaction 5.31 to 5.89 (p<0.01). Psychological safety 5.38 to 5.65, not significant. Workload (NASA-TLX) 3.93 to 4.12, not significant. Juniors stayed lower than seniors in both conditions.
limits: Self-report, not decision accuracy; small N; short CHI late-breaking work; seniors said they ignored the agent over time.
agent_relevance: Satisfaction is not correctness. Do not cite this as evidence that LLM red teaming improves decisions.

source: Bohnet et al. (2025) Enhancing LLM planning capabilities through intrinsic self-critique
finding: A counter-example to Huang: iterative self-critique raised planning accuracy a lot, with no external verifier, on structured planning tasks.
numbers: Blocksworld 3-5 blocks: 49.8% to 89.3% (Gemini 1.5 Pro). Blocksworld 3-7: 57.2% to 79.5%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 68% to 89.5%. Logistics hard set 18.9% to 32.8%. Gemma-2 27B: no gain on Blocksworld.
limits: Few-shot and many-shot prompting base; October 2024 checkpoints; plan rules are checkable from the text; small model did not improve.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: self-critique can work when the task has explicit rules the model can re-check and the model is large. Not proof for open-ended judgment.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction studies: unfair evaluations inflate results. Success needs reliable external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three findings: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
limits: Survey as of mid-2024; Bohnet 2025 is later and partly cuts against (1).
agent_relevance: Design rule: the critic's evidence must come from code, tests or retrieval, not from the same model's opinion (G2, G10).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Splits red teaming into finding the flaw and fixing it. Finding is the weak part; fixing is strong once the location is given.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 chain-of-thought traces from PaLM 2 with the first error located. Best model (GPT-4) found the mistake location with only 52.87% accuracy under direct step-level prompting. With the true location given, word-sorting backtracking fixed 23.53% of wrong-answer traces and broke 11.11% of right-answer traces.
limits: Traces sampled 85% wrong, 15% right; objective tasks; five models tested.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: the model fixes well once code shows where the fault is. Spend effort on locating faults by execution, not on asking for criticism.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: A model judging its own output is biased toward it, and the bias grows with how well it recognises its own writing.
numbers: All three models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2) beat 50% at telling their own summaries from others without fine-tuning; fine-tuning on 500 examples gave over 90% self-recognition for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2; self-preference scaled linearly with self-recognition.
limits: Summarisation tasks; preference, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: A red team made from the same model is a weak outsider. Strengthens G5: critic sees no authorship.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?
finding: Failure taxonomy (MAST) built from 1600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks. Failure rates were high even in systems built on role-play and review.
numbers: Failure rate between 41% and 86.7% across seven open-source multi-agent systems; 21 traces human-annotated, three annotators for agreement on a 15-trace set; rest labelled by an LLM judge.
limits: Open-source frameworks and chosen benchmarks; annotation partly by LLM.
agent_relevance: Adding reviewer or critic roles does not make a system reliable; failures often come from role handoff design.

source: Mandel & Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Structured analytic techniques (the family that includes alternative analysis and red-team style challenge) were mandated by law in 2004 and spread by prestige, not by testing.
numbers: Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act 2004 mandated SATs; ICD 203 (2015) requires analysts to use reasoning techniques that 'reveal and mitigate bias'. No controlled accuracy trial of ACH is cited.
quote: The SAT paradigm has spread not because there is evidence it works
limits: Perspective article, not an experiment; argues by hypothesis.
agent_relevance: The field has almost no measured evidence that red teaming improves judgment. Our claim must come from our own tests (G7).

source: Mandel & Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Heuer, who built Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, argued testing was unnecessary. The authors call this the 'goodness heuristic'.
numbers: Quoted 2010 post by Heuer: asks whether one cannot be confident by common sense that assessing the inconsistency of evidence improves analysis, and says he would ignore a test that did not replicate exactly how ACH is used.
limits: Single quoted source.
agent_relevance: Warning for our own work: a technique that feels sound is not evidence. Test red-team steps against the plain model at equal tokens (G7).

source: Mandel & Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: One-directional warnings (beware overconfidence, beware confirmation) may shift the response threshold and produce the mirror bias: underconfidence and endless second-guessing.
numbers: Cites underconfidence in strategic intelligence forecasts (Mandel & Barnes 2014, 2018) and in analysts' experimental probability judgments (Mandel 2015). No new data.
limits: Hypothesis; applies to humans.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Huang: a doubt prompt can swing the agent into flipping good answers. Measure both error directions.

source: Mandel & Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: SATs are weakly defined multi-step processes that leave many choices to the analyst, so they can add noise (unreliable judgments) while claiming to remove bias.
numbers: Admiralty-code study (Mandel 2018 annex): agreement among analysts fell as source-reliability and information-credibility ratings became mismatched. ACH cell scoring can mean likelihood, inverse likelihood, necessity, plausibility or representativeness.
limits: Few extant noise studies; the ACH claim is argued, not measured.
agent_relevance: Procedures with vague steps are a source of variance. Our red-team step needs a fixed, code-checked definition of 'a challenge passed'.

source: Wikipedia: Red team (history and military practice)
finding: Military red teaming grew from 1960s RAND/Cold War simulations. Ipcha Mistabra was set up in Israel after 1973; the US Army Directed Studies Office (red team) in 2004; UFMCS trains red teamers (6 to 9 weeks for Marines). The article offers no measured effect on decisions.
numbers: TSA red-team agents got weapons or fake explosives through screening 67 of 70 times in 2015. The 2011 bin Laden raid used three red teams. No outcome metric reported for military planning.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia source; used only for dates and the absence of measurement.
agent_relevance: Real-world evidence is of two kinds: red teams find weaknesses in systems (clear), and red teams improve plans (unmeasured). We can borrow the first.

source: Schwenk (1990) Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of laboratory studies of assigned-dissent methods. Devil's advocacy beat the expert-only approach in general. Dialectical inquiry was not shown better than the expert approach on ill-structured tasks. Neither beat the other.
numbers: Pooled effect sizes and number of studies not obtained; only abstract-level statements seen in a search snippet.
limits: Mostly student groups on small case tasks.
agent_relevance: Assigned dissent has modest support in human groups on structured tasks, weaker on ill-structured ones.

source: Nemeth, Brown, Rogers (2001) Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent
finding: Role-played devil's advocacy is weaker than real dissent. Authentic dissent stimulated more thoughts and solutions; assigned devil's advocacy can make people hold their original view more firmly (from a secondary source).
numbers: Numbers not read. The secondary source (Wikipedia citing Nemeth 2018 book) says assigned dissent is 'considerably less effective' than authentic dissent.
limits: Primary text blocked (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: A critic told to argue a side is not a critic with a different real view. For an LLM, 'different' may mean a different model or different evidence, not a persona (G4).

source: Lord, Lepper, Preston (1984) Considering the opposite: a corrective strategy for social judgment
finding: Telling people to 'be fair' did not reduce biased reading of mixed evidence, but asking them to consider the opposite did.
numbers: Effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Not opened; recall only.
agent_relevance: Specific, directed instruction ('what would make the opposite true') beats general warnings. Supports signal-triggered, concrete challenge over a general 'be critical' line.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events
finding: Imagining that an event has already happened (prospective hindsight) increased the number of correct reasons given for the outcome by roughly 30% versus ordinary forecasting. Basis of the premortem.
numbers: About 30% (widely cited; not re-checked).
limits: Not opened. Tests reason generation, not plan quality or later outcomes.
agent_relevance: A premortem is a cheap concrete challenge: assume failure and list causes. Candidate for S3 when a signal fires.

source: Herzog & Hertwig (2009) The wisdom of many in one mind: dialectical bootstrapping
finding: A second estimate made after 'assume your first was wrong' is partly independent of the first. Averaging the two beat either alone. A cheap internal red team with a measured gain in people.
numbers: Gain size not retrieved; later replications (e.g. Fraundorf & Benjamin 2016, not read) are reported to find smaller or conditional gains.
limits: Not opened; recall only.
agent_relevance: The model analogue is an independent second sample. G4 says same-model samples are correlated, so expect weaker gain than in people.
